title: Cognitive Biases in UX Research
intro: Your brain is working against your research. 20 cognitive biases quietly distort how you collect, interpret, and present UX findings — and most teams never notice.

learn.title: How we misjudge people
learn.text:
Three biases shape how you see the humans in your research:

**Implicit bias** — Unconscious assumptions about groups. You assume an older user isn't tech-savvy, then interpret their hesitation as incompetence instead of a confusing UI.

**Attribution error** — Blaming personality when circumstances explain behavior. A talkative user doesn't explore more features because they're chatty — they explore more because the facilitator gave them extra time.

**False consensus** — Assuming others share your mental model and vocabulary. You label a button "Configure" because it makes sense to you — but users search for "Settings."

right.label: What's actually happening
items: The UI is confusing for anyone new

try.q: A user struggles with your prototype. You think: "They're just not very technical." Which bias is this?
try.explain: Attributing their struggle to who they are (implicit bias) rather than what your design does wrong.

learn.title: How we fool ourselves
learn.text:
The most dangerous biases affect your own reasoning:

**Confirmation bias** — You only log evidence that supports your hypothesis. You remember the 3 users who struggled with checkout but forget the 5 who sailed through.

**Watch your language:** Saying "validate the design" frames research as proving you're right. Say "evaluate" or "test" instead. Aim to be proven wrong — that's where the insights are.

**Torres's rule:** Always test multiple ideas in parallel — never just one. If you only evaluate one solution, confirmation bias guarantees you'll find reasons to love it. Comparing three ideas forces you to notice each one's weaknesses.

**Sunk cost fallacy** — Resisting a fix because "we already built this." Testing reveals a flaw, but the team doubles down because redesigning feels wasteful.

**Motivated reasoning** — Treating one Medium article as equal to decades of research with tens of thousands of participants, because the article confirms what you already believe.

**Recency bias** — Changing your design based on one recent interview that contradicts many earlier ones.

left.label: Do this
items: Judge fixes on current evidence, not past effort
Weigh evidence by quality and volume
Compare new findings to the full body of research

right.label: Not this
items: Cherry-pick quotes that match your hypothesis
Refuse to redesign because it took 3 sprints
Cite a blog post to override field data
Pivot the design after one surprising interview

try.q: Testing reveals a clear usability issue, but your team says: "We spent 6 weeks on this — we're not changing it." Which bias?
try.explain: Sunk cost fallacy — continuing because of investment already made, not because the evidence supports the current design.

learn.title: Biases in the research itself
learn.text:
Some biases are baked into how you run sessions:

**Social desirability** — Users overstate positive behavior. "I'd use this feature all the time" usually means "I want to be polite."

**Self-reporting bias** — A user calls a task "easy" after failing to complete it. What they say and what they do are different data.

**Framing effect** — Telling a participant "others found this hard" changes how they approach the task.

**Serial-position effect** — Items at the start and end of a list seem more important. Your dropdown order shapes what gets picked.

Biases rarely appear alone. A single team discussion dismissing a usability finding can involve five biases at once.

**What to do:** Keep a shared reference of these biases. Check the list when a gut feeling seems off.

try.q: A user rates your prototype 9/10 but couldn't finish the main task. Which bias explains the gap?
try.explain: Social desirability — they're being polite and don't want to seem negative, even though their behavior tells a different story.

test.q: You only record interview quotes that support your hypothesis. Which bias is this?
test.explain: Confirmation bias — seeking or recording only evidence that supports what you already believe.

test.q: A teammate says: "Our power users don't need labels on icons — they're advanced." No data supports this. Which bias?
test.explain: Power-user fallacy — assuming heavy users behave differently without data to back it up.

test.q: After a failed usability test, a user says: "Oh yeah, I knew that button was wrong the whole time." Which bias?
test.explain: Hindsight bias — rationalizing the past as if the outcome was always obvious.

test.q: You change your entire design direction based on one recent interview, even though 8 earlier sessions said the opposite. Which bias?
test.explain: Recency bias — overvaluing the newest information at the expense of the larger body of evidence.

test.q: According to the article, how should teams use awareness of cognitive biases?
options: Keep a shared reference and check it when gut feelings seem off
Assign a 'bias officer' to each project
Run a bias-elimination workshop before every sprint
Avoid qualitative research to reduce bias exposure
test.explain: The article recommends a shared reference document you can check during decisions, onboarding, and intense projects — not eliminating research or creating new roles.
